newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy takes long-awaited step to free gold mkt.
newsitem.headline: Italy takes long-awaited step to free gold mkt.

text.p: Italy took a long-awaited step to liberalise its domestic gold market on Friday when the government drafted a law to abolish the state's monopoly.
Analysts said the move to do away with the state's stranglehold on gold bullion trade was overdue and inevitable but needed to see details of how the new system would operate.

A cabinet statement said the draft, which must now go to parliament, included provisions to exempt bullion operations from Value Added Tax. Transactions would be liable to capital gains tax and operators would have to declare deals of 20 million lire ($12,000) or more in line with current regulations.
"It's premature to talk of setting up a real and proper Italian gold exchange but it could be a first step," said a Milan-based international gold market source.
"In Italy, the market for gold bullion as a private investment is practically non-existent. The only way individuals could buy it has been in the form of jewellery," he added.
Italy is the world's leader in gold jewellery making.
The statement, issued after the cabinet met to approve the draft, said the provisions would bring Italian rules on gold trading in line with European Union directives on free commerce.
"The measure defines which professionals can operate in the sector, including banks, which must meet specific requirements of professionalism, honourability and reliability," it said.
Under existing provisions, all trade in gold bullion has to be conducted through the Bank of Italy or its appointed agents.

Agostino Roverato, Chairman of the Italian goldsmiths' federation which represents an industry using some 400 tonnes of gold a year, said: "We are very happy the government has finally approved this draft law, but we await further details."
Philip Klapwijk, principal analyst at Gold Fields Mineral Services in London, said the government's move had been inevitable but many questions remained unanswered.
"It really all depends on the detailed arrangements, the type and number of institutions allowed to trade gold on a VAT-free basis," he said.

"The government's statement talks of bringing Italy into line with Europe but there isn't a common European Union standard for gold. At the EU level there are moves afoot to come up with common standards, but there is no norm. The system and VAT rates are different in member countries."
But he said the move would certainly help liberalise trade in gold products and bullion with other EU members where currently there are restrictions on gold imports.
Analysts said it was not yet clear to what extent the gold jewellery industry would be involved, noting that jewellery manufacturers were not included in the British bullion market.

"At the moment there only a handful of banks active in the Italian bullion market. Everyone is wondering will it include the larger jewellery manufacturers and refiners. Which route will the authorities go down," Klapwijk noted.
"There is also enormous scope for fraud," he said. "Individuals could go into a bank and buy an ingot saying it was for investment and then make it into gold products."
One analyst who declined to be named added: "In Italy there is the fear that gold will be used as a means of capital flight.
"The Italian authorities are scared of the scope for money laundering, and this has delayed the move to liberalise the market," he said. ($=1,659 lire)
